Sparsity
Too little room to read a ranking. The report and its settings are retained.

Sparsity

Axiom's other analysis pane. It and Ontology Quality do the same shape of work and looked nothing alike: 51 of its rules still came from the original styles.css, it has no row in the per view policy table, and SparsityPanel.tsx never wraps AdaptivePane, so it had no size behaviour at all. This makes the two read as one family.

The settings region is the Quality geometry, reused rather than reinvented

Four rows at 32 pixels plus an action line at 36, 164 pixels at every width. A settings row never wraps; its content column scrolls. Drag the pane narrow and watch a row scroll rather than double in height, which is the only reason a height budget can be enforced at all. The action sits at the end of the settings it commits, not pushed to the far edge by a flexible spacer.

The method is the published one, implemented

This is not a stand in score. docs/sparsity-analysis.md specifies the measure and the pane computes it: for each candidate among the children of a parent, the direct child count against the mean of its other siblings, the descendants at shortest distances 2, 3 and 4 discounted by 1, 0.5 and 0.25 against the same baseline, each deficit as max(0, 1 - candidate / peer mean), and the score as 100 times the weighted mean. Descendant influence is adjustable from 0 to 40 percent and, as written, a zero deeper peer mean puts the whole weight on direct children. The worked example in that document holds here: a root with A at five children and B at one gives B 80 and A 0.

The rest of the published behaviour is intact: ranked findings, select to inspect, navigation to Hierarchy or Details, text filtering, a minimum score defaulting to 25, leaf inclusion, paging in groups of 40, settings retained with the workspace, and a worker that makes no RDF edits. Classes in cycles are excluded and the exclusion is reported rather than silently applied, and a lone child is left unscored because it has no baseline.

Three things the rebuild adds

The baseline is visibleSelect a finding and the sibling group it was measured against opens underneath it, with every sibling's direct child count and the mean. The published document asks for exactly this: "Select a finding to see its direct child count beside its siblings." Without it a score is an assertion. With it the reading small peer groups and unusually large siblings should be considered becomes something you can actually do.
The score is never colour aloneEvery row carries the number, a bar and a word. The bar is the fastest to scan and the least reliable, so it is third in the reading order and the first thing to withdraw when the pane narrows.
Findings are grouped by the comparison that produced themEvery score is relative to one sibling group, so the group is the row's context, not decoration. It also makes multiple inheritance legible: a class under two parents is compared once under each, and appears under both.

What is seeded rather than read from your store

The taxonomy here is generated: 12 top branches, deliberately uneven development, one class with two parents and one two class cycle so the exclusion path is real rather than described. Every number on screen is computed from that tree by the method above, including the breadth first descendant counts. Against your ontology the numbers would differ; the measure would not.
